summaries.example: Imagine a long strip of paper divided into boxes. A tiny rule-following helper looks at one box, reads its mark, changes the mark if needed, moves left or right, and changes its internal state. If the rules say to write 1, move right, and use the next rule, the helper does exactly that. With suitable rules, it can make a repeating pattern such as 010101.
summaries.summary: A Turing machine is a very simple imaginary computer. It has a row of boxes called a tape, a reading head, a small number of states, and exact rules. At each step, it looks at its state and the symbol in the box, writes a symbol, moves, and changes state. This simple setup helps philosophers and computer scientists ask what computation really is. Turing's original machines were connected with calculating numbers and with a major question about logic: whether one general method could decide every statement in a certain logical system. Later versions changed details, such as the tape's direction and the way instructions are written, but these versions have the same basic computing abilities. A universal Turing machine can imitate any other Turing machine when it is given that machine's coded rules. This shows how a program can be treated as information. The model also reveals limits: some questions, including the general question of whether every machine will eventually stop, cannot be solved by one all-purpose method.
key_ideas: A Turing machine is an imaginary machine, not a machine built from metal and wires.
Its action is controlled by its current state and the symbol it is reading.
The tape is treated as having unlimited room, and a computation may be allowed unlimited time in theory.
Different-looking versions of Turing machines can still compute exactly the same kinds of things.
Some problems cannot be solved by any Turing machine.
summaries.why_it_matters: Turing machines give us a clear way to think about computers without getting distracted by the parts of a particular device. They help explain both the power and the limits of algorithms. The idea of a universal machine also helps us understand general-purpose computers: one machine can follow many different programs. The model is idealized, because real computers have limited memory and time, but that idealization helps show what is possible in principle and what is impossible even for a computer with unlimited resources. It is also important to remember that the history of modern computers involved many people and developments, not just one inventor.

important_terms.definition: A simple mathematical model used to study what can be worked out by following exact instructions.
One of the machine's few possible situations, such as being ready to start or checking the next box.
A long row of boxes that can hold marks. The machine reads and changes one box at a time.
A small instruction that tells the machine what to write, where to move, and which state to use next.
A problem or task for which some exact set of instructions can always produce the right answer, if given enough time and space.

summaries.example: Consider a machine that receives two natural numbers in unary notation: the number 3 is written as four 1s, and the number 4 as five 1s, with a 0 separating the blocks. Its transition rules can erase one extra 1, turn the separator into a 1, move through the tape, and eventually leave one block representing 7. The example shows that a computation depends not only on rules but also on an interpretation of the symbols and on agreed starting and finishing configurations.
summaries.summary:
Turing machines were introduced as abstract devices for clarifying the idea of an effective procedure. In the original model, a machine has finitely many internal configurations, a one-way infinite tape divided into squares, and a head that scans one square at a time. Its next action is fixed by the current state and scanned symbol: it may print, move left or right, remain in place, and enter another state. Post proposed a related formulation with more atomic instructions, one kind of symbol, a two-way infinite tape, and a state in which the machine halts. Modern definitions often use a finite set of states and symbols together with a transition function.

A complete configuration records the tape's finite data, the head's location, and the current state. Listing successive configurations describes the machine's dynamics. To connect formal symbol manipulation with useful calculations, an interpretation must be supplied; for example, blocks of 1s may represent numbers. Turing's universal machine extends this idea by encoding another machine's program on its tape and imitating that machine. Thus, program and data can be handled as symbol sequences by the same formal device.

The philosophical importance of the model comes from the Church-Turing thesis, which identifies Turing computability with effective computability. This is not an ordinary theorem, because it connects a precise formal notion with an informal one. The model nevertheless has strong support from the equivalence of several independently developed formalisms. It also reveals limits. Through diagonal-style arguments and reductions, one can show that problems such as the halting problem are not computable. key_ideas: Turing's original formulation used a one-way infinite tape, finite states, symbols, and rules whose actions were determined by the current state and scanned symbol.
Post's reformulation separated printing from moving, removed Turing's special F- and E-square arrangement, and used a two-way infinite tape with a halting condition.
A modern formal definition can represent a machine as states, symbols, an initial state, and a transition function.
A machine's behavior can be represented by successive instantaneous descriptions, not merely by its final output.
The universal machine depends on coding both programs and configurations as strings that can be copied, marked, compared, and erased.
The model distinguishes computability in principle from computability in practice, and it supports proofs that some decision problems are uncomputable.
summaries.why_it_matters: Turing machines provide a common language for discussing algorithms, programs, machines, and impossibility results. Their importance is not that real computers literally use an infinite tape, but that the model isolates basic features of step-by-step symbolic computation. It helps distinguish what is computable from what is merely feasible with available resources. The universal-machine idea also illuminates the principle that instructions and data can occupy the same memory and be manipulated by the same system. important_terms.definition: A formal model with finitely many states and symbols, an initial state, and a transition function that determines each next step.
A function that maps a current state and scanned symbol to a replacement symbol, a movement, and a next state.
A complete description of a computation at one moment: tape contents, head position, and internal state.
The claim that every effectively computable process can be carried out by a Turing machine, or by an equivalent formal model.
A problem is reducible to another when a method for solving the second can be turned into a method for solving the first.
The problem of deciding, for every machine and input, whether the machine eventually stops.
A Turing machine able to imitate the behavior of any other Turing machine when given a description of its rules.

summaries.example: Suppose a robot has a strip of boxes marked with 0s and 1s. It starts in state A and looks at the first box. A rule might say, “If you are in A and see 0, write 1, move right, and switch to state B.” Another rule tells it what to do in state B. By choosing rules carefully, the robot can make the pattern 010101 without understanding the pattern the way a person does.
summaries.summary:
A Turing machine is a deliberately simple model of computation. It has a tape divided into squares, a reading head, a finite collection of states, and a finite set of rules. At each moment, the rule selected by the current state and scanned symbol determines what happens next. The machine may write a symbol, move, and change state. Because the rules are exact, there is no need for an outside person to make choices during an ordinary, deterministic computation.

Turing introduced this kind of machine while investigating whether there could be a general method for deciding every statement in a certain part of logic. Post later proposed a related version. His changes included using simpler separate actions, one type of tape symbol, a tape extending in both directions, and an explicit way for a machine to halt. These differences matter historically and conceptually, although the standard versions are equivalent in what they can compute. A formal description can replace the picture of a tape with sets of states and symbols plus a transition function. To describe what a machine is doing, we record an instantaneous description: its tape contents, head location, and internal state.

Turing also developed the idea of a universal machine. A program can be encoded as a string of symbols, placed on a tape, and processed by another machine. The universal machine then imitates the steps of the encoded machine. This is a striking connection between programs and data. It helps explain why one general-purpose computer can perform many different tasks.

key_ideas: Turing machines are models for studying computation, not descriptions of one particular physical computer.
The machine's behavior is determined by its current state and the symbol under its reading head.
Turing and Post gave related definitions, but they differed about the tape, symbols, instructions, and stopping.
A full snapshot of a computation includes the tape, the head's position, and the machine's state.
The universal machine shows that a program can be written as data and then examined or imitated.
Some tasks are not computable, even though a Turing machine may have unlimited time and tape in theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: This model matters because it gives computer science and philosophy a precise way to ask what algorithms can and cannot do. It separates two questions: whether a task is possible in principle and whether it is practical with limited memory and time. The universal machine explains a central feature of general-purpose computing: the same device can behave differently when supplied with different programs. The model also shows that some limits are not caused by slow hardware. Certain problems, such as the halting problem, cannot be solved by any single algorithm of the required general kind. important_terms.definition: An imaginary computer made from a tape, a reading head, symbols, states, and exact step-by-step rules.
A label for the machine's current situation. The next action depends partly on this label.
A rule that tells the machine what to write, how to move, and which state to enter next.
A task that can be completed by a precise procedure, at least when unlimited time and memory are allowed in the model.
A machine that can copy the work of any other Turing machine after receiving a coded description of its rules.
The question of whether a machine will eventually stop rather than continue forever.
